content: The French Revolution was a transformative period of political and societal upheaval in France, beginning with the convening of the Estates General—a representative assembly of the three social classes— in 1789 and concluding with the Coup of 18 Brumaire, when Napoleon Bonaparte seized power on 9 November 1799. The Revolution’s central purpose was to challenge the absolute monarchy and the entrenched privileges of the nobility and clergy, aiming to establish a society based on the principles of liberty, equality, and fraternity. Key causes included widespread social inequality between the estates, political conflict over representation and authority, and severe economic hardship marked by fiscal crisis and food shortages. Major phases of the Revolution included the fall of the Bastille, the abolition of feudalism, the Reign of Terror, and the rise of the Directory government. The Revolution’s ideals—such as popular sovereignty, secularism, and the rights of citizens—became foundational to liberal democracy and continue to shape debates on citizenship, secularism (laïcité), and social justice in modern French political discourse. Ultimately, the French Revolution profoundly altered the course of French and world history, laying the groundwork for modern democratic institutions and values.
